Decentralized control for a heterogeneous UAV-UGV swarm doing search and rescue in collapsed buildings and forests needs to be scoped around five tightly coupled subsystems: per-agent state estimation that also senses victims and hazards, real-time decentralized role assignment, failure-tolerant task reallocation, an intermittent ad-hoc mesh for critical-information sharing, and a simulation-based evaluation plan with quantitative guarantees.

For per-agent state estimation, a proven building block is extended-Kalman-filter fusion of an IMU, a monocular camera, and a 2D LiDAR to produce full 3D pose estimates for a single UAV in an unknown GPS-denied environment, validated in both simulation and real flight tests. [00508_44376]
This kind of fusion generalizes to ground platforms too, since legged locomotion frameworks for quadrupeds such as HyQ combine perception-driven foothold planning, whole-body torque control, and disturbance observers to traverse debris, ramps, and stairs, which is directly relevant to a UGV role in rubble. [00150_74098]
Critically, the same onboard sensor suite used for SLAM can double as a detection pipeline: autonomous mine-rescue aerial robots fuse LiDAR, thermal vision, and inertial cues for GPS-denied localization and mapping while a deep-learning classifier searches the reconstructed volumetric map for survivors and associated objects such as backpacks or phones. [04776_37580]
A complementary, non-vision detection layer combining CO2/O2 gas sensors, a microphone with SVM-based voice-activity detection, and a thermal camera successfully localized a simulated buried casualty in eight of nine trials within about one hour in a high-fidelity collapsed-building test site, illustrating a concrete multi-modal victim-detection metric. [01548_68906]
At the system level, DARPA's Subterranean Challenge showed that heterogeneous robot teams operating without GPS or reliable communications could still generate maps differing from expert ground truth by under one percent in under an hour, evidence that fused multi-sensor autonomy scales to kilometer-length unstructured environments. [02399_20431]

For decentralized role assignment, several mechanisms avoid any central coordinator while remaining formally analyzable.
A minimal-communication approach lets robots switch between roles such as mapping, searching, or clearing purely through probabilistic transitions triggered by local encounters with other robots, converging to a desired task distribution without any explicit messaging. [00563_70316]
The Consensus-Based Bundle Algorithm and its Partial-Replanning extension provide a decentralized, peer-to-peer auction that provably converges to a near-optimal, conflict-free allocation in O(nt·D) communication rounds and can absorb newly discovered tasks, like a fresh hazard report, without a full team-wide re-solve. [01135_37566]
A collision-aware auction variant adds a proven fifty-percent optimality lower bound while explicitly discouraging robots from being assigned overlapping paths, which matters when UAVs and UGVs share the same corridor of a collapsed structure. [04197_13192]
Because CBBA-style consensus is itself message-intensive, a communication-aware extension learns which agents should transmit or stay silent based on local network density, improving convergence specifically in communication-constrained, ad-hoc environments like the one this proposal targets. [01476_21025]
When agents are lost or degraded rather than merely delayed, a resilient task-allocation framework reoptimizes robot-to-task assignments based on measured capability degradation, exhibiting graceful performance loss rather than catastrophic failure. [02654_73087]
More broadly, resilient multi-robot coordination under robot failure is formally NP-hard, but bounded approximation algorithms built on robust submodular optimization and network reconfiguration can still guarantee a fraction of optimal reward while restoring team connectivity after losses. [03811_73292]
A real heterogeneous deployment validating this division-of-labor idea is the Emesent–CSIRO Data61–Georgia Tech SubT team, which fielded drones, tracked crawlers, and quadrupeds that explored autonomously while sharing local map data over a self-formed wireless mesh network, with Georgia Tech supplying the coordination and division-of-labor framework across the fleet. [03235_74753]

For propagating victim locations, hazards, and blocked passages over a dropping mesh, distributed mapping systems and disaster-tuned routing protocols are the relevant building blocks.
Kimera-Multi, MIT's distributed multi-robot SLAM system, lets robots exchange map data with semantic annotations whenever they come within communications range, incrementally building a single globally consistent map without any central server. [04181_27198]
DiSCo-SLAM achieves the same goal more cheaply by fusing lidar and inertial odometry on each robot and exchanging only lightweight scan-context descriptors at rendezvous points, keeping bandwidth use low even for large 3D point-cloud maps. [05590_5558]
At the protocol layer, teams in DARPA's Subterranean Challenge learned to drop battery-powered mesh-network nodes like breadcrumbs as robots advanced, restoring connectivity after early tunnel-circuit tests in which robots lost contact after the first bend. [02399_20431]
Purpose-built disaster routing such as Disaster-Optimized Spray-and-Wait, a delay-tolerant-network protocol, prioritizes high-urgency messages so that victim and hazard alerts are delivered with higher probability while keeping the overhead ratio roughly constant despite intermittent connectivity. [03994_56216]
Quantitatively, comparisons of AODV, BCHP, and DSDV mobile ad-hoc routing protocols show that control-message overhead can consume thirty to sixty percent of total throughput, with cluster-based BCHP delivering the best overhead-to-reliability tradeoff, a useful baseline for reporting network overhead in the proposed evaluation. [00849_25010]

For the effectiveness analysis, the strongest available empirical precedent is a decentralized, behavior-based UAV swarm that located over ninety percent of survivors in under one hour in disaster-realistic simulations while continuing to operate through individual robot failures or crashes, closely matching the target ninety-percent-within-bounded-time metric. [02295_23124]
A related evaluation pattern deliberately disables robots mid-mission to observe how a distributed mapping "colony" degrades, which is a directly applicable methodology for stress-testing coverage and victim-finding rate under a thirty-percent agent-loss condition. [04540_75585]
For a more formal treatment, probabilistic real-time schedulability analysis offers a template for bounding the probability that a mission deadline is missed, using probabilistic worst-case response-time distributions compared against an acceptable failure-probability threshold rather than a hard worst case. [00025_35157]
Combining this schedulability-style threshold argument with the bounded-approximation guarantees for resilient coordination under failures gives a plausible formal backbone for a claim like "ninety percent of reachable victims within bounded time under thirty percent agent attrition," though the committed evidence does not include a paper proving that exact joint bound, which remains an identified gap to close analytically or through additional targeted simulation.
